meta.study: CPG Cranberry synthetic primary market research — synthesis
meta.mandate: HUMAN VALIDATION MANDATE: All respondents are synthetic AI-generated personas. Findings are hypotheses only and must be validated with real human interviews, smoke tests, and sales tests before any business decision.
meta.status_rules: Validated >= 60% Supports; Invalidated <= 20% Supports AND majority (>50%) Contradicts; otherwise Partially Validated.
meta.coding_rules: Supports = expresses the assumed behavior/attitude without major conditions; Partial = conditional or context-limited (e.g., gift only, only if low sugar); Contradicts = explicitly rejects or cannot picture it.

biggest_unmet_need.title: A genuinely satisfying, low-sugar 'afternoon slump' treat that is actually indulgent — real-fruit tartness, no crash, portable
biggest_unmet_need.description: The strongest, most widespread unmet need is not 'a luxury cranberry snack' but a treat for the weekday afternoon slot (and away-from-home moments) that feels indulgent yet does not deliver a sugar crash, bloat, or a 'chalk/sand' health-food disappointment. Every respondent recounted a recent disappointment with a snack that promised more (health, protein, 'gourmet', pretty) than it delivered, and most describe the afternoon as a defined, emotionally loaded moment currently served by chocolate, dates, mango, pastries or vending/minibar options they find 'meh' or 'depressing'. Cranberry can compete for this slot only if it is tart-forward, verifiably low in added sugar, and in a portable/resealable format — none of which the current 'sweet white cranberry, design-forward' concept yet proves. This is a hypothesis to test with real consumers, not a validated finding.
evidence: 10/10 Q2 disappointments were a snack that over-promised (8 'protein'/'healthy' snacks; Priya's 'gourmet' trail mix; Chloe's pretty pistachio bar), described as chalk/sand/drywall/eraser/candle wax.

8/10 describe a defined afternoon snack moment (Sienna, Maya, Priya, Zoe, Olivia, Hannah, Rachel, Lauren); Sienna: 'It's honestly the most important snack of my day.' Zoe and Hannah both call it 'the danger zone'.

Dissatisfaction with current away-from-home options: Maya's office snack wall ('meh'), Priya's hotel minibar ('just so depressing'), Hannah's break-room pastries, Olivia's sugar crash from a coffee-shop bar.
8/10 raise sugar/label concerns; Sienna: 'No sugar crash, no bloating, no guilt spiral… That's really the bar for anything that becomes a daily thing for me.'

7/10 like tart flavors unprompted (Q8) but reject 'sugar with acid' candy-sour; 6/10 could picture the concept in a personal afternoon/desk slot, all conditionally (Sienna, Chloe, Maya, Priya, Olivia, Hannah).

runner_up_signals.title: Non-generic hostess / small-gift tin (the 'anti-Godiva')
evidence: The only contexts where price clears $9 for Priya ($18 EC/$28 TE) and Daniel ($15/$20) are gifts.
All 5 respondents with a 3-pack ceiling >= $24 (Sienna, Chloe, Priya, Olivia, Daniel) are in gift/hosting contexts.
Priya: 'I refuse to show up with Godiva. It feels like you grabbed it at the airport.' Daniel: 'The worst outcome is spending $40 on something that looks like I grabbed it at a CVS.'
Caveat: Maya, Priya, Rachel, Lauren tie cranberry gifting to November–December — this signal pulls toward seasonality.

runner_up_signals.title: Tart / sour / salty-spiced flavor profile (li hing mui, amla, chili, yuzu, sour-coated)
evidence: Maya: 'If it tasted like a sour plum kind of thing, salty-tart, that would get my attention way more than "white cranberries."'
Priya wants 'a tart version, maybe with chili or something, like an amla candy' and says 'sweet cranberry' is 'solving the wrong problem'.
Zoe: 3pm only 'Unless it was sour, like a sour-coated cranberry thing'; Sienna: 'If it's actually tart and they lean into that, I'm more into it.'
7/10 enjoy tart unprompted; 4 explicitly see 'sweet' as the wrong direction. Counter-signal: Rachel (kids) and Lauren want sweet/less bitter.

runner_up_signals.title: Cheese-board / entertaining pairing
evidence: 8/10 first or most easily pictured a board/party moment at Q14.
Lauren: 'tart fruit makes sense next to something rich and salty'; Sienna: 'Cranberry and cheese already makes sense'.
Suggests cheesemonger-counter sampling (Lauren: Citarella cheesemonger next to a Stilton) and hosting use — but hosting is occasional, and Priya reports leftover dried fruit going to waste.

runner_up_signals.title: Verified low-sugar / blood-sugar-friendly tart treat
evidence: Olivia: 'If you could say "doesn't spike you" and prove it, that would honestly matter more to me than the packaging or the white cranberries.'
8/10 sugar concern; Olivia's threshold 'under five grams'.

implications.title: Do not build the model on weekly habit; treat recurrence as unproven and lead with trial + gifting
implications.evidence: A3 Invalidated: 0/10 support, 9/10 contradict; stated behavior 7 Try once, 3 Occasional gift, 0 recurring. Zoe: 'good for your first month and then we're gone'.
implications.validation_needed: Real repeat-purchase data: sell at a Happier Grocery pop-up/shelf test for 8–12 weeks and track repeat rate by customer (loyalty/QR/email capture); DTC cohort with 30/60/90-day reorder tracking. Kill/pivot threshold set in advance (e.g., <20% 60-day repeat).

implications.title: Re-anchor self-purchase price below the $9–16 band; reserve $9+ and $24+ for gift formats
implications.evidence: Self EC median $8 (mean $8.50); self too-expensive median $12.50; 8/10 have a self too-expensive threshold <= $16; only 4/10 have self EC >= $9; 5/10 would pay >= $24 for a 3-pack, all gift-only.
implications.validation_needed: Van Westendorp + Gabor-Granger with n>=100 real target shoppers; price-ladder smoke test (landing page / paid social A/B at $7, $10, $14 single and $24/$32 gift trio); in-store price test at Happier with actual units sold.

implications.title: Break the 'fancy Craisins' frame with product truth, not packaging: tart-forward, low added sugar, sugar grams on the front
implications.evidence: 10/10 said 'fancy Craisins'; 8/10 sugar concern; Olivia: 'paying extra for sugar feels like being played'; 7/10 like tart; Priya/Sienna/Maya/Zoe see 'sweet' as the wrong direction.
implications.validation_needed: Blind sensory tests (real people, n>=30 per cell) of tart/salty-tart, chili-lime, sweet white cranberry vs. Craisins and a Hu square; measure liking and 'would buy again'; confirm achievable added-sugar level with a food scientist before making claims.

implications.title: Keep the white cranberry as the hook, but prove what it does (less sugar needed? less bitter?)
implications.evidence: The only element that created curiosity (9/10); 4 make its value conditional on less sugar/bitterness; Lauren asks 'whether that's real or a gimmick'.
implications.validation_needed: Supply and sensory validation of white cranberries (availability, cost, Brix/acidity vs. red); claim test in real interviews: 'white cranberry' vs. 'white cranberry, naturally less tart, X g added sugar'.

implications.title: Drop 'small batch / handmade' and 'everyday treat' claims; replace with specific provenance
implications.evidence: 10/10 discounted 'small batch'; 3 read it as 'expensive', Daniel as 'inconsistent'; 8 doubted 'everyday treat'; Sienna and Lauren want a named farm / real person.
implications.validation_needed: Message A/B tests on paid social and in-store shelf talkers (named-farm story vs. small-batch vs. none), measuring click-through, add-to-cart and purchase, not stated preference.

implications.title: Sampling-led go-to-market: every buyer is a 'once' buyer until they taste it
implications.evidence: 10/10 framed purchase as 'once'; 5 explicitly said a sample would change their decision (Maya, Priya, Hannah, Rachel, Lauren); Hannah: 'I'll eat a free one and then decide'; Lauren trusts shopkeepers, not ads.
implications.validation_needed: In-store demos at Happier Grocery and cheese counters (Citarella/Eataly), office/clinic sample drops; measure sample-to-purchase conversion and 30-day repurchase versus non-sampled shoppers.

implications.title: Design: elegant and understated beats 'cute'; packaging earns trial, not loyalty
implications.evidence: Packaging mattered in some context to 9/10, but 0/10 said it drives repeat and 4 said explicitly it won't; 3 reject 'cute/pastel' outright (Priya, Olivia, Lauren); 7 express 'paid for the wrapper' distrust.
implications.validation_needed: Shelf/visual preference test with real shoppers (cute pastel vs. understated tin vs. minimal clinical) measuring pick-up and purchase; separate gift-buyer and self-buyer cells.

implications.title: Recurring requires weekly channels and passes the household economic buyer
implications.evidence: 8/10 would need it in a store they shop weekly or on subscription (TJ's, Whole Foods, Target, H-E-B, Thrive, Costco); Happier is a weekend/monthly 'treat trip' for Maya, Hannah, Rachel; Daniel approves/cancels subscriptions on price per ounce; Rachel's kids gate the list.
implications.validation_needed: Subscription pre-order smoke test with deposit; dyad interviews with couples/households (discoverer + payer); retailer buyer conversations (Whole Foods/Erewhon) on velocity requirements.
